# Behind the Scenes at the 81st Academy Awards

In our Behind the Scenes series, CNN correspondents share their firsthand experiences covering the news and offer insight into the stories behind the headlines. Here, CNN's Jay Kernis reflects on what it was like inside the Kodak Theatre during the Academy Awards.

*Hugh Jackman, host of the 81st Academy Awards, addresses the audience at the Kodak Theatre on Sunday evening.*

**LOS ANGELES, California (CNN)** -- From the comfort of your living room, it's easy to be critical. But inside the theater, the entire show comes alive—especially the grand production numbers. Perhaps this year's ceremony was simply exceptionally well-produced, but from within the audience, you feel genuinely part of the spectacle, even from the heights of the second mezzanine.

I've covered the Oscars from the outside before, but this marked my first time attending the ceremony itself. I brought along my 17-year-old son, Noah, for the experience.

Arriving on the red carpet, you first pass through a security tent, presenting your ticket and driver's license. Inside, you notice the tent divided by red velvet ropes, and with practiced, genial efficiency, celebrities are guided to one side while everyone else is directed to the other. This ensures that stars exit closer to the waiting cameras—and any illusion that everyone in a gown or tuxedo stands as equals for the evening quickly fades away.

*View scenes from the Oscars »*

Curious what happens during commercial breaks? Stagehands wielding powerful flashlights orchestrate swift set and curtain changes, while ensuring any empty orchestra seats are promptly filled. Host Hugh Jackman took a moment to introduce his parents to the crowd, and a short film celebrating the magic of cinema—one that had been cut from the broadcast—was shown to those in attendance. At one point, Jackman handed his wife a plate of cookies, sensing she might be hungry, and later revealed that the cellist performing with the Academy Award Orchestra was none other than actor Dermot Mulroney. Who knew?

*Watch a report on the night's big winners »*

The evening shone brightest when it reminded us that Hollywood still excels at what it has always done best: captivating an audience and holding its attention. Watching five former Best Actor winners share the stage to present the award was nothing short of extraordinary. Equally striking was Sean Penn's genuine self-awareness upon winning Best Actor.

The Oscars can still leave you in awe—proving they still know how to stage a spectacular musical number, complete with a hundred dancers in top hats moving with the precision of a Busby Berkeley routine. And they still know how to touch the heart: when Heath Ledger's parents and sister accepted his posthumous award, they spoke of celebration—though one can't help but imagine they would have far preferred to see him accept it himself.

Amid all the dazzling special effects Hollywood can conjure, and despite the abundance of star power filling the theater that night, there was something truly remarkable about witnessing Philippe Petit in person—the daring wire walker who, in 1974, spent 45 suspended minutes traversing the space between the Twin Towers. Watching him balance an Oscar statuette on his chin brought a rare and unexpected moment of pure joy.

# Inside the Oscars: A Different Perspective

CNN's Behind the Scenes series gives viewers a glimpse into how correspondents experience news firsthand and uncover the deeper narratives behind major events. Correspondent Jay Kernis offers his personal account of attending the Academy Awards ceremony at the Kodak Theatre. During the 81st Academy Awards, host Hugh Jackman addressed the crowd gathered at the venue on Sunday evening.

LOS ANGELES, California (CNN) -- Watching from your living room, it's easy to nitpick and judge harshly. But once you're actually seated in the theater, everything clicks into place—particularly the elaborate musical numbers. Perhaps this year's production was simply exceptional, but there's an undeniable sense of belonging that washes over you as an audience member, regardless of how far back you're sitting.

Despite years spent reporting on the Oscars from outside, this marked my first opportunity to actually witness the ceremony from within. My son Noah, age 17, accompanied me for the experience.

Getting inside means passing through a security checkpoint where your ticket and ID are checked. What catches your eye is how the tent space is divided by velvet rope barriers—staff members smoothly direct famous faces to one side while everyone else goes to the other. This arrangement positions celebrities closer to the waiting cameras as they exit, quickly dispelling any notion that all the glamorously dressed attendees share equal status for the evening.

Curious about what unfolds during those commercial breaks? Crew members wielding bright flashlights work quickly to rearrange sets and adjust curtains, while ushers fill any vacant seats in the orchestra section. Meanwhile, Jackman took a moment to introduce his mother and father to the crowd, and a brief film celebrating cinema's impact—one that didn't make the final broadcast—played for the live audience. At another point, Jackman brought his wife some cookies, apparently sensing she needed a snack, and later revealed that the cellist performing with the Academy Award Orchestra was none other than actor Dermot Mulroney—a fact few in attendance would have guessed.

The evening shone brightest when it showcased Hollywood's enduring talent for captivating audiences—witnessing five former Best Actor winners share the stage to present an award was truly remarkable, as was Sean Penn's genuine, self-aware acceptance speech after winning Best Actor.

The ceremony proved it hasn't lost its magic touch: the ability to stage a jaw-dropping musical spectacle, complete with a hundred performers in top hats executing precisely choreographed routines reminiscent of Busby Berkeley's classic style. It also proved capable of delivering emotional gut-punches—when Heath Ledger's parents and sibling accepted his posthumous award, they framed it as a celebration of his work, though one suspects they would have far preferred him being there to accept it himself.

Amid all the dazzling visual effects Hollywood can produce and despite the theater brimming with star power that night, perhaps the most extraordinary moment came from watching Philippe Petit take the stage in person—the daredevil who famously walked a tightrope between the Twin Towers for 45 minutes back in 1974. Seeing him playfully balance his Oscar statuette on his chin brought an unexpected touch of pure delight to the evening.

CNN correspondent Jay Kernis recently shared a uniquely personal account of attending the 81st Academy Awards, offering readers an insider's perspective that only firsthand attendance could provide. Kernis brought along his 17-year-old son, Noah, transforming what could have been a routine assignment into a memorable shared experience between father and son at Hollywood's most glamorous event.

## A Different Perspective From the Second Mezzanine

One of the most striking revelations from Kernis's account was how dramatically different the experience felt compared to watching from home. Even seated in the second mezzanine—far from the prime orchestra-level seats reserved for A-list celebrities—Kernis and his son found themselves swept up in the energy of the live production. This is a stark contrast to the experience of watching on television, where viewers often adopt a critical, detached stance, dissecting fashion choices and speeches from their couches. Being physically present in the Kodak Theatre, Kernis explained, created a sense of communal participation rather than passive observation. The audience became part of the show's fabric, reacting in real-time to the same dramatic pauses, surprises, and emotional moments that television viewers would only see edited and packaged after the fact.

## The Hidden Hierarchy of the Red Carpet

Kernis's report also pulled back the curtain on the red carpet experience, revealing subtle but unmistakable class distinctions among attendees even before the show began. Velvet ropes—those seemingly innocuous decorative barriers—actually serve a much more calculated purpose: they physically separate A-list celebrities from other attendees, including press, industry professionals, and lesser-known guests. This arrangement ensures that stars are positioned closer to the cameras, guaranteeing maximum photographic and video coverage of the biggest names while relegating others to a more peripheral role in the visual narrative of the evening. It's a small but telling detail that underscores how meticulously choreographed every aspect of the Oscars truly is, extending far beyond the stage itself.

## Behind-the-Scenes Chaos and Charm

Perhaps the most captivating portion of Kernis's account details the frantic, often overlooked activity that occurs during commercial breaks—moments invisible to the television audience but very much part of the live experience. It's a delightful reminder that awards shows, for all their scripted glamour, still harbor moments of genuine surprise and hidden talent waiting to be discovered by attentive audience members.

Through Kernis's engaging firsthand account, readers gain valuable insight into the layered, multifaceted experience of attending the Academy Awards in person. From the subtle class distinctions embedded in red carpet logistics to the frenetic backstage energy during commercial breaks, and even surprising celebrity cameos in unexpected roles, the 81st Academy Awards emerges as a far richer and more complex event than its polished television broadcast suggests. # Behind the Curtain: My First Oscars Night

I've watched the Academy Awards on television for as long as I can remember, but nothing quite prepared me for the experience of sitting in the Dolby Theatre and witnessing Hollywood's biggest night unfold in person. As a CNN correspondent, I've covered plenty of red carpets and press junkets, but this was different—this was the main event, and I was inside the room where it actually happens.

The security procedures alone were an education in themselves. Getting into the theater felt more like preparing for a flight to a high-security nation than attending an entertainment awards show. Multiple checkpoints, thorough bag searches, and credential verifications happened at every turn. Once inside, the level of coordination required to manage thousands of attendees, hundreds of press members, and the actual production of a live broadcast watched by millions became immediately apparent.

What struck me most, though, was what happens during commercial breaks—the moments television audiences never see. When the cameras cut away for advertisements, the theater transforms. Stage managers rush across the floor with clipboards, barking instructions to crew members. Presenters who were composed and camera-ready moments before suddenly relax, chatting with neighbors, checking phones, or making quick trips to grab water. The tension that builds during live segments dissipates into a kind of controlled chaos, only to snap back into professional polish the instant the broadcast resumes.

This stage management is a choreographed dance that requires split-second timing. I watched producers signal countdowns with fingers, watched winners get gently but firmly guided offstage when their speeches ran long, watched the orchestra conductor poised and ready to strike up music at a moment's notice. It's a live event with all the unpredictability that entails, yet somehow it comes together into the polished broadcast we see at home.

But perhaps the most valuable insight from attending in person is how fundamentally different the live experience is from watching on television. There's an immersive quality to being in that room—feeling the collective gasp when an upset occurs, hearing the genuine laughter ripple through the audience, sensing the anticipation before a major award is announced—that simply doesn't translate through a screen. You become a participant rather than merely an observer, caught up in the emotional current of the room alongside everyone else.

This proximity also reveals candid, human moments that get lost in the broader broadcast narrative. I watched Hugh Jackman, in a break between segments, warmly introduce his parents to those seated nearby, beaming with the kind of pride any son would show off camera. Later, in another unguarded moment, I saw him playfully feeding his wife cookies, a small tender gesture that had nothing to do with performance and everything to do with genuine affection. These weren't moments crafted for the cameras—they were glimpses of real people who happened to be surrounded by Hollywood's most recognizable faces.

These small, authentic instances underscore something important about the entertainment industry that skeptics sometimes forget: despite all the glamour, scripted moments, and carefully managed publicity, there's still something genuinely captivating about watching artists and performers exist as themselves, even briefly. Hollywood's enduring appeal isn't just about the films or the fashion—it's about these fleeting glimpses of humanity breaking through the spectacle.

Leaving the theater that night, I found myself with a newfound appreciation for an event I'd watched countless times from my couch. Television captures the highlights, the winners, the speeches—but it can never fully capture the electric, unpredictable energy of being there, surrounded by thousands of people sharing in a moment of collective celebration. That's an experience no broadcast, however well-produced, can truly replicate.

# Behind the Scenes at CNN: How News Gets Made

CNN, one of the world's most recognizable news networks, operates a complex machine that most viewers never see. Behind the polished broadcasts and breaking news alerts lies an intricate ecosystem of journalists, producers, technicians, and editors working around the clock.

## The Newsroom Floor

At the heart of CNN's operation is the newsroom—a bustling space filled with dozens of monitors displaying live feeds from around the globe. Producers scan wire services, social media, and correspondent reports simultaneously, making split-second decisions about what makes air and what gets cut. The energy is often described as controlled chaos, especially during breaking news events when normal schedules are thrown out the window.

## The Control Room

Perhaps the most fascinating hidden space is the control room, where directors coordinate camera angles, graphics, audio levels, and satellite feeds in real time. A single broadcast might involve:

- Multiple camera operators positioning shots
- Graphics teams building lower-thirds and data visualizations on the fly
- Audio engineers balancing sound from remote correspondents
- Technical directors switching between dozens of video sources

## The People You Don't See

While anchors like Anderson Cooper or Wolf Blitzer become household names, thousands of employees work without on-camera recognition:

- **Field producers** who negotiate access in dangerous conflict zones
- **Fact-checkers** verifying information before it airs
- **Researchers** building context for breaking stories
- **Camera crews** risking safety to capture footage in war zones or natural disasters

## The Pressure of 24/7 News

CNN pioneered round-the-clock news coverage when it launched in 1980, and that model demands constant vigilance. Staff work in shifts to ensure coverage never stops, meaning someone is always monitoring global events at 3 a.m., ready to break into programming if major news occurs.

## Editorial Decisions

Behind every story lies editorial judgment—what to cover, how to frame it, which experts to interview. These decisions happen in meetings throughout the day, often under intense time pressure, balancing accuracy, viewer interest, and journalistic responsibility.

Understanding what happens behind the scenes at CNN reveals the tremendous effort required to deliver news that appears seamless to viewers but represents countless hours of preparation, technical expertise, and split-second decision-making.

**Behind the Scenes: Inside the Kodak Theatre for Oscar Night**
*A CNN Correspondent's Notebook*

HOLLYWOOD, California — By the time I reached my seat in the mezzanine press section of the Kodak Theatre, I had already passed through three security checkpoints, had my bag swabbed for explosive residue, and walked past enough LAPD officers and bomb-sniffing dogs to make you forget, briefly, that you were here to watch people in gowns hand each other gold statues.

That's the thing about covering the Academy Awards from inside the room: the glamour is real, but so is the machinery underneath it. This year — the 81st Academy Awards, with Hugh Jackman hosting and "Slumdog Millionaire" the odds-on favorite — that machinery felt more visible than ever.

**Getting In**

My credential process began nearly 48 hours before the ceremony. Press badges are color-coded and tiered — where you're allowed to stand on the red carpet, whether you get access to the theater interior, whether you're confined to the Fan Bleachers or the print risers — and each level requires its own background check. On the day of the show, credentials were checked no fewer than five times between the perimeter fencing on Hollywood Boulevard and my actual seat.

The security footprint around the Kodak swallows several blocks. Streets close a full day in advance. Snipers are visible on rooftops if you know where to look. Every vehicle entering the secure zone — including the shuttle vans ferrying press from satellite parking — gets checked with mirrors underneath and a walk-through with the dogs. It's easy to forget, watching the broadcast at home, that this is technically one of the most heavily fortified few blocks in America for one night a year.

**The Room Itself**

Inside, the theater is smaller and steeper than it looks on television — more like a Broadway house than the airplane-hangar magnitude I'd imagined. The show runs with military precision because it has to: ABC's broadcast is timed to the second, and a stage manager with a headset spends the entire evening standing just off-camera making frantic "wrap it up" gestures at anyone whose speech runs long. I watched the orchestra conductor, cued by producers, strike up the exit music on at least four winners this year — a not-so-subtle hint that gratitude has a shot clock.

Commercial breaks, it turns out, are the real show for anyone sitting in the room. The moment the broadcast cuts away, stagehands sprint out in packs to reset risers, swap microphones and reposition cameras, all while a warm-up comedian works the crowd to keep energy up. Seat-fillers — mostly young industry hopefuls in rented tuxedos and borrowed gowns — dash into any empty chair the second a nominee steps out to the bathroom or a smoke break, so the cutaway shots never show a gap. During one break I watched a seat-filler practically vault over an armrest to claim a spot next to Meryl Streep before the return-from-commercial countdown hit zero.

**The Moments You Don't Get on TV**

Some things only land differently in the room. When Heath Ledger's family came up to accept his posthumous Best Supporting Actor award for "The Dark Knight," the ovation didn't feel like television applause — it went on long enough that you could feel, physically, the room deciding together not to stop. People around me were openly in tears, including colleagues who'd covered a dozen Oscar ceremonies and sworn they were unshockable by now.

Sean Penn's win for "Milk" produced an entirely different kind of charge — a ripple of laughter through the room at his crack about "commie, homo-loving sons of guns," followed by a more serious hush as he pivoted to talk about equality. You could feel the room split slightly along political lines in real time, something the cameras don't quite capture.

And the format change this year — bringing out five past winners to individually address each acting nominee before the envelope opened — visibly caught some nominees off guard. From where I sat, you could see actors mouthing "oh my God" as the presenters turned toward them one by one. It added ten minutes to an already marathon show, but in the room, it was the most emotionally unguarded stretch of the night.

**The Long Walk Out**

When it finally ended — just past midnight, after "Slumdog Millionaire" swept eight awards including Best Picture — the exit was its own logistical event. Winners are peeled off toward the Governors Ball and press rooms through separate corridors from everyone else, while the rest of us funnel back out through the same checkpoints we'd entered, credentials scanned once more on the way out, as if the building needed proof we were leaving with the same number of people we came in with.

Walking back out onto Hollywood Boulevard, past the barricades finally being folded up and the bomb-sniffing dogs finally off duty, it struck me how strange the contrast is: three hours of the most heavily produced, tightly controlled broadcast in America, built on top of a night that — underneath the security and the stagecraft — still comes down to a room full of people getting genuinely emotional about a little gold man.

That's the version you don't quite get at home. And it's why, every year, it's worth being in the room.

# Inside the Academy Awards: A First-Timer's View From the Audience

**HOLLYWOOD** — There's a moment, just before the lights dim inside the Dolby Theatre, when the room seems to inhale collectively. I felt it Sunday night, seated a level up from the orchestra floor, my 16-year-old son beside me clutching a program he'd already dog-eared with predictions.

This was my first time attending the Oscars in person, not watching from a newsroom monitor or scrolling reaction on a second screen. And the experience of sitting inside that gilded auditorium — rather than covering it from the outside — reframes everything you think you know about Hollywood's biggest night.

## The View Most Viewers Never See

Television makes the Oscars look seamless: category to category, joke to joke, tears to triumph. Sitting in the audience reveals the machinery underneath.

During commercial breaks — and there are many, stretching the broadcast well past three hours — the theater transforms. The moment the red "ON AIR" signs go dark, an army of stagehands in black materializes from the wings. They move with the choreographed urgency of a pit crew, swapping out set pieces, repositioning cameras on tracks that snake through the aisles, adjusting flowers on the front-row tables reserved for nominees.

My son, who plays trombone in his high school jazz band, was fascinated by the crew wrangling musicians for the In Memoriam segment, testing microphone levels while stanchions were wheeled away. "It's like halftime at a football game," he whispered, "except everyone's wearing tuxedos."

Handlers with earpieces hustled presenters into position off-stage, running through blocking one more time. A woman with a clipboard mouthed countdowns to no one in particular. Someone re-touched a bit of gold paint on a statuette replica used for a bit that never made air.

## The Room Reacts Differently Than You'd Think

What surprised me most was the audience itself. Categories that generate Twitter firestorms — animated short, documentary categories — often draw the loudest, warmest applause in the room, even as television audiences use those moments to refill drinks. Meanwhile, some of the night's biggest "surprises" register barely a ripple in person, because industry insiders had already clocked the outcome through weeks of guild awards.

My son, going in as a devoted fan of one of the Best Picture nominees, admitted afterward that watching from inside changed his relationship to the ceremony. "You can see how much it means to people who aren't the famous ones," he said — the sound editors, the costume designers, walking to the stage on legs that seem to remember, suddenly, that millions are watching.

## A Night He Won't Forget

By the time the final award was handed out and the crowd spilled toward the exits, past armfuls of gift bags and champagne flutes, my son had filled the margins of his program with notes he'll probably never look at again — but he'll remember, I suspect, the geography of it all: where he sat, who walked past, the particular hush before a winner's name is read aloud.

For one night, at least, the Oscars felt less like a broadcast and more like church — ritual, reverence, and a fair amount of stagehands in black, keeping the miracle running on time.

# Behind the Scenes: A Correspondent's Notebook from Oscar Night

*By Jay Kernis, CNN*

There's a moment every Oscar season when the chaos of red carpet cables, camera flashes, and rehearsed soundbites suddenly gives way to something real. This year, it happened for me somewhere between the orchestra pit and the wings of the Kodak Theatre, watching a room full of the most photographed people on the planet fall completely silent.

I've covered the Academy Awards for CNN for several years now, and I've learned that the broadcast people see at home is a different animal entirely from what unfolds backstage. The show is a live, breathing organism—and this year, it had a pulse unlike any I'd witnessed before.

**A Host Who Understood the Assignment**

Hugh Jackman opening the show wasn't just a hosting gig—it was a statement. In a year when the industry was nervously eyeing shrinking budgets and a changing entertainment landscape, Jackman came out swinging with an old-Hollywood song-and-dance number that felt both nostalgic and defiant. Backstage, stagehands who'd seen it all were mouthing the lyrics along with him on the monitors. That's when you know someone's landed it.

I caught him for maybe ninety seconds in the wings before his second segment. He was breathing hard, grinning, already thinking about the next transition. "Just trying to remind people why we love this stuff," he told me. That sentiment ran through the whole night.

**Sean Penn's Quiet Intensity**

When Sean Penn's name was called for Best Actor, I was stationed near the press room, watching the monitors alongside photographers who'd already predicted the win. But predicting it and witnessing it are different things. Penn's speech—raw, political, unapologetically his own—reminded everyone why he's one of the most fearless actors of his generation. Backstage afterward, reporters pressed him on his comments. He didn't flinch. He rarely does.

**The Moment Nobody Wanted to Rehearse**

But if you ask me what I'll remember most about this particular ceremony, it's not a moment of celebration. It's the collective breath the room took when Heath Ledger's name was announced for Best Supporting Actor.

# Inside the Kodak Theatre: What the Cameras Don't Show You

LOS ANGELES — For years, I watched the Oscars the way most Americans do: sprawled on a couch, remote in hand, occasionally fast-forwarding through the technical categories to get to the moments that matter. I thought I understood the rhythm of the show—the tension before an envelope opens, the sweep of a camera across a sea of famous faces, the way the whole night seems to unfold with cinematic precision.

I was wrong. Watching from home is like reading a postcard description of a mountain range. Sitting inside the Kodak Theatre is like standing at the summit.

## The Room Breathes Differently

The first thing that surprises you is the scale—and the lack of it. The Kodak Theatre is far more intimate than the television broadcast suggests. Camera angles create an illusion of vastness, of stars scattered across a distant galaxy. In person, you realize you could toss a program a few rows and hit a face you've seen forty feet tall at your local multiplex.

But intimacy comes with static. The audience doesn't experience the show as a continuous stream the way home viewers do. Commercial breaks aren't invisible pauses—they're loud, floodlit intermissions where the temperature in the room seems to rise, where publicists dart through the aisles repositioning their clients, where you can watch a nominee's practiced smile falter into something more human before the cameras click back on.

At home, the Oscars feel inevitable, seamless. Inside the theater, you see the machinery—the stage managers with headsets, the frantic hand signals, the sheer logistical improbability that this thing comes together at all.

## The Sound You Can't Hear on TV

Television flattens emotion into something manageable, packaged for a living room. In the theater, you feel the room's collective intake of breath before a major category. You hear the laughter that doesn't quite make it to the broadcast mix, the murmurs of surprise, the genuine gasps that get lost somewhere between the microphone and your television speaker.

There's also an unfiltered quality to the reactions. A joke that lands awkwardly gets a different kind of silence in person than the one you sense through your screen. You feel embarrassment, delight, and boredom moving through the room like weather systems—informing, in real time, how the show is actually landing, rather than how it's being edited to land.

## Then, Suddenly: A Man on a Wire

Nothing captured the strange magic of live theater more than the moment Philippe Petit took the stage.

Petit—the French high-wire artist who, in 1974, illegally strung a cable between the still-unfinished towers of the World Trade Center and walked between them, an act of astonishing audacity later immortalized in the documentary "Man on Wire"—had just watched that film win the Oscar for Best Documentary Feature.

What happened next wasn't in any script I could have anticipated from my living room. Petit, ebullient, seemingly unable to contain himself, produced a coin and appeared to balance it on his chin, then attempted a bit of impromptu balancing with an Oscar statuette itself—delighting an audience that had, moments before, been politely clapping through another acceptance speech.

On television, this likely read as a charming few seconds of levity—a palate cleanser before the next category. Inside the theater, it was electric. It was the sudden, unrehearsed reminder that spontaneity still has a place in an evening otherwise engineered down to the second. The room's laughter wasn't the polite, anticipatory laughter of a well-timed joke. It was surprised laughter—the kind that comes from watching a wire-walker refuse, even for a moment, to leave the tightrope behind.

That's the thing about being there in person: you don't just witness the show. You witness the show discovering itself, in real time, alongside you.

## What Gets Lost in Translation

The Oscars broadcast is a masterclass in narrative control—six-second reaction shots, orchestrated pacing, music cues that tell you exactly how to feel about a montage. It's built, quite deliberately, to be consumed from a couch.

But sitting in the Kodak Theatre reminds you that underneath all that polish is something messier and more alive: a room full of people—famous and anonymous alike—experiencing genuine surprise, discomfort, joy, and tedium in real time. Philippe Petit balancing an Oscar on his chin wasn't a moment television could fully capture, because television isn't built to capture accidents. It's built to capture outcomes.

The next time you watch the Oscars from your couch, remember: you're seeing the finished postcard. Somewhere in that room, a thousand small, unrepeatable moments are happening that no broadcast will ever fully convey.
